samples.summary: Server-exemption compares resolved addresses, so an image on the CLI's own server is blocked when the two spellings resolve to different loopback families (::1 vs 127.0.0.1)
samples.evidence: `allowed = addresses.filter(a => exempt.has(a.toLowerCase()) || (!internalName && !isPrivateAddress(a)))`. With `--server http://localhost:3000` and a document storing the absolute `http://127.0.0.1:3000/images/<id>` (the frontend persists absolute srcs), `addresses = ['127.0.0.1']` while `exempt = serverAddresses(localhost)`. On a host where `dns.lookup('localhost', {all:true})` answers only `::1` (IPv6-preferring/Docker setups), exempt = {'::1'}, the fallback arm rejects 127.0.0.1 as private, `allowed` is empty and `assertFetchableImageUrl` throws IMAGE_URL_BLOCKED — the export of a document whose images live on the configured server fails. Identity matching is per-address only; no loopback-equivalence is applied.

samples.summary: `isOpaqueRedirect` treats any status-0 response as an opaque redirect and silently re-issues the hop through real undici, bypassing the injected `fetch` seam
samples.evidence: `return res.type === 'opaqueredirect' || res.status === 0;` — `Response.error()` (a genuine network-failure response, type 'error', status 0) also satisfies this, and line 595 then calls `rawRequest(target, agent)`, which issues a *second, real* network request through `undiciRequest`, ignoring `opts.fetch`. A caller-supplied transport that signals failure with `Response.error()` therefore gets a duplicate live request instead of a classified failure (the new test at test/image-fetcher.test.ts:~'opaque-filters it' relies on exactly this conflation).

samples.summary: `rawRequest` throws an unclassified TypeError for null-body statuses (204/205/304)
samples.evidence: `new Response(Readable.toWeb(res.body) as ReadableStream<Uint8Array>, { status: res.statusCode, headers })` — Node's Response constructor rejects a non-null body with a null-body status (204, 205, 304), throwing `TypeError: Response with null body status cannot have body`. `Readable.toWeb` always yields a non-null stream, so a 304/204 hop taken through the fallback path escapes as a bare TypeError (no `code`, no `exitCode`) and is reported as a generic exit-1 'ERROR' rather than the classified failure the surrounding contract promises.

samples.summary: `fetchLoginSession` parses each response body with an unguarded `.json()`, so a 200 with a non-JSON body escapes the login exit contract
samples.evidence: `const tokens = (await exchangeRes.json()) as {...}` (and the identical `meRes.json()` / `wsRes.json()` at lines 147 and 162) have no `.catch`. A 200 carrying HTML (captive portal, proxy interstitial, truncated body) rejects with a SyntaxError, which `classifyLoginFailure` returns `null` for, so it is rethrown, loses the prose path and surfaces as a stack trace with exit 1 — while the same server condition is documented as a system error. `HttpClient.sendJson` guards the equivalent call with `.catch(() => null)`.

samples.summary: `process.exit(exitCode)` immediately after `console.error` can truncate the message when stderr is a pipe
samples.evidence: `console.error((e as Error).message); process.exit(exitCode);` — writes to a piped (non-TTY) stderr are asynchronous in Node, and `process.exit()` does not flush pending writes. Under `wafflebase login 2>log` or when run from an agent harness the failure message can be lost, leaving only the exit code. Setting `process.exitCode` and returning would preserve it.

samples.summary: The 401 response body is never drained/cancelled before the refresh-and-retry, leaking the undici connection; the API-key endpoints now take this path too
samples.evidence: In `send()`, after `res.status === 401` the code calls `refreshSession()` and then re-fetches, but the first `res` body is never read or cancelled. undici keeps the socket alive until the body is GC'd. Pre-existing, but this change routes `listApiKeys`/`createApiKey`/`revokeApiKey` through `send()` for the first time (lines 388-399), widening the paths that leak.

samples.summary: The 'too many redirects' message reports the original URL, not the hop that exceeded the limit
samples.evidence: `throw blocked(\`Image fetch failed: too many redirects for ${redactUrl(resolved)}\`)` uses `resolved` while every other message in the loop uses `target`. A redirect chain is diagnosed by where it ended, not where it started, so the message points at the wrong URL.

finding.summary: Server-exemption compares resolved addresses, so an image on the CLI's own server is blocked when the two spellings resolve to different loopback families (::1 vs 127.0.0.1)
finding.evidence: `allowed = addresses.filter(a => exempt.has(a.toLowerCase()) || (!internalName && !isPrivateAddress(a)))`. With `--server http://localhost:3000` and a document storing the absolute `http://127.0.0.1:3000/images/<id>` (the frontend persists absolute srcs), `addresses = ['127.0.0.1']` while `exempt = serverAddresses(localhost)`. On a host where `dns.lookup('localhost', {all:true})` answers only `::1` (IPv6-preferring/Docker setups), exempt = {'::1'}, the fallback arm rejects 127.0.0.1 as private, `allowed` is empty and `assertFetchableImageUrl` throws IMAGE_URL_BLOCKED — the export of a document whose images live on the configured server fails. Identity matching is per-address only; no loopback-equivalence is applied.

verdict.reason: The quoted line exists verbatim at image-fetcher.ts:322-325 and matches the exempt set by exact lowercased string only; serverAddresses (:253-264) just lowercases resolved addresses into a Set, and neither isPrivateAddress (:155-199) nor parseIPv6 (:122-152) applies any loopback-family equivalence across addresses. The failing path is concretely reachable: for --server http://localhost:3000 and a doc src http://127.0.0.1:3000/..., internalName is false (isInternalHostname :76-84 matches names only), mayBeServer is true (:307-308), addresses = ['127.0.0.1'] via the literal shortcut (:219-220), and exempt = lookup('localhost'). If that answers only ::1, exempt.has('127.0.0.1') is false and isPrivateAddress('127.0.0.1') is true (127/8 at :100), so allowed is empty and :328-332 throws IMAGE_URL_BLOCKED, failing export of the document's own server-hosted images. No caller guards it — createImageFetcher invokes assertFetchableImageUrl unconditionally per hop (:581). The module's own comment (:241-252) states the exemption exists precisely so different spellings of the server are not refused, so this is a broken stated invariant, not intended strictness. Existing tests (test/image-fetcher.test.ts:317-355) all stub localhost to ['127.0.0.1'], so the single-family/::1 case is untested rather than handled. I found no ground (not-present, already-guarded, out-of-scope, counterexample) to refute on; the only open question is how often a host resolves localhost to one family, which is frequency, not correctness.

finding.summary: Image downloads now force a per-request undici `Agent`, silently bypassing any globally configured dispatcher (HTTP/HTTPS proxy)
finding.evidence: `createImageFetcher` builds `pinnedAgent(addresses)` and passes it as `dispatcher` on every hop (`{ redirect: 'manual', ...(agent ? { dispatcher: agent } : {}) }`). An explicit dispatcher overrides undici's global dispatcher, so a proxy installed via `setGlobalDispatcher(new ProxyAgent(...))` or Node's `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` handling is ignored: the connector dials the resolved IPs directly. Worse, on a machine that can only reach the internet through a proxy the gate's own `defaultLookup` (`dns.lookup`) and the direct connect will both fail, so `docs/slides export` of any document containing an external image now fails with `NETWORK_ERROR` where it previously succeeded through the proxy. Nothing in the change restores the ambient dispatcher's proxy settings on the pinned agent.

verdict.reason: The finding's central premise is not present in the code. The per-hop dispatcher is `hopDispatcher(target, addresses)` (image-fetcher.ts:582), not `pinnedAgent(addresses)`. `hopDispatcher` (image-fetcher.ts:393-410) calls `proxyForUrl(target)` first and returns `new ProxyAgent(proxy)` (line 400) whenever the environment configures a proxy for that URL, falling back to the address pin only for direct connections (line 409). `proxyForUrl` (lines 456-473) implements the conventional surface — `no_proxy` bypass, `https_proxy`/`http_proxy` by scheme, then `all_proxy`, each read in both lower- and upper-case spellings via `envValue` (line 413) — which is the same variable set Node's NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY handling consults, so the proxy is honored rather than bypassed, and `ProxyAgent` is imported from the same `undici` used for fetch/request (line 6). The claim "Nothing in the change restores the ambient dispatcher's proxy settings" is directly contradicted by lines 371-410, whose comment names the exact failure mode ("on a machine whose only route out is a proxy every external image in a document would fail to export") as the reason the branch exists; tests at packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts:486-542 cover it. The only residual — a programmatic `setGlobalDispatcher` being outranked — has no call site in packages/cli/src (grep finds `setGlobalDispatcher` only in explanatory comment text at line 451), and both production call sites (commands/docs.ts:273, commands/slides.ts:214) build the fetcher inside the CLI binary, so the asserted NETWORK_ERROR export regression does not follow.
